pos: n. (Johannes Bugenhagen, 1485–1558, called Pomeranus, pastor of the town church at Wittenberg, Luther's confessor, and organiser of the Reformation in north Germany and Denmark)
etymology: German surname; Pomeranus from Pomerania, his homeland.
biblical_def: Johannes Bugenhagen was a priest and schoolmaster in Pomerania who read Luther's Babylonian Captivity in 1520, at first thought it the worst heresy ever written, then came to Wittenberg and became one of the Reformation's quiet builders. For more than thirty years he was pastor of St Mary's, the town church, and Luther's own confessor and pastor; he married Luther and Katharina von Bora, and preached at Luther's funeral. His gift was order. He wrote church orders for Brunswick, Hamburg, Lübeck, Pomerania and Denmark, setting out preaching, catechising, schools, poor relief and the calling of ministers, and in 1537 he crowned King Christian III and reorganised the Danish church. Paul's charge to Titus describes the work: “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). He saw ministers as Paul did, “as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1Co 4:1). He also helped Luther revise the German Bible and translated it into Low German. As a confessor he practised the old mutual counsel of James, “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another” (Jas 5:16), stripped of the sacrament of penance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines order as regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; established method; and, in ecclesiastical use, a rule or regulation for the conduct of worship and discipline.
webster_full: ORDER, n. Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things.
2. Proper state; condition in which things belong.
3. Established process; method.
scriptures: Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.
Jas 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Bugenhagen is the forgotten pastor of the Reformation, and his neglect reflects a modern preference for heroic stands over the slow work of ordering churches.
corruption_paragraphs: Histories of the Reformation tell of Luther at Worms and Calvin at Geneva; few remember the pastor who wrote the church orders that actually reshaped the life of congregations across northern Europe. The modern church shares the bias, prizing visionary leadership and dramatic renewal and neglecting the patient construction of catechesis, discipline, schools and care for the poor that makes a reformation last.

The recovery is to honour stewards. Paul told Titus to set in order what was wanting, and the doing of it is as much a gift of Christ to His church as the preaching that began it. Bugenhagen's church orders taught generations to hear the Word, learn the catechism and care for the poor.
roots_summary: Greek epidiorthoo (G1930), to set in order; oikonomos (G3623), steward; exomologeo (G1843), to confess.
roots_lines: Greek epidiorthoo (G1930) — to set further in order; Titus 1:5, the only use.
usage: “set in order the things that are wanting” (Tit 1:5) — the work of the church orders.
“stewards of the mysteries of God” (1Co 4:1) — Bugenhagen's idea of the ministry.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — a Reformation that lasted.

pos: n. (Matthias Flacius Illyricus, 1520–1575, Lutheran theologian who resisted the Interims, led the Magdeburg Centuries, wrote the first Protestant hermeneutics, and erred in calling original sin the substance of fallen man)
etymology: Latin form of the Croatian Vlačić; Illyricus from Illyria, his birthplace at Labin in Istria.
biblical_def: Matthias Flacius came from Istria to Wittenberg, was delivered from despair by Luther's counsel, and became professor of Hebrew. When the emperor imposed the Interims after 1548 and Melanchthon accepted Roman ceremonies as things indifferent, Flacius left Wittenberg for Magdeburg and declared that nothing is indifferent in a time of confession, when yielding is taken as surrender. His ground was Paul's at Jerusalem: “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5). He directed the Magdeburg Centuries, the first great Protestant church history, to show that the true church had never wholly died, and his Key to the Holy Scriptures was the first Protestant treatise on interpretation. But in controversy with Victorinus Strigel he insisted that original sin is not an accident in man but his very substance, the image of the devil. Paul distinguishes the man from the sin: “it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me” (Rom 7:17). The Formula of Concord rejected Flacius's formula, and his own party broke over it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines indifferent as neutral; not inclined to one side more than the other; and, in morals, neither good nor evil in itself.
webster_full: INDIFFERENT, a. Neutral; not inclined to one side, party or thing more than to another.
2. Unconcerned; feeling no interest, anxiety or care respecting any thing.
3. Having no influence or preponderating weight; of no account; neither good nor evil in itself.
scriptures: Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Rom 7:17
Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me.
Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: Flacius was right that things indifferent cease to be indifferent when a persecutor demands them as a sign of submission, and wrong to make sin the substance of man; both lessons are needed now.
corruption_paragraphs: The adiaphora controversy is not ancient history. Whenever the state or the culture demands a gesture that seems small — a pinch of incense, a pronoun, a ceremony — Christians are told it is a thing indifferent and that resisting it is fanaticism. Flacius answered that in a case of confession the indifferent thing becomes a confession of the other side. That is Paul refusing to circumcise Titus, not for an hour.

His error about original sin was the zeal of the same temperament pressed too far. If sin is man's substance, then the Son could not take our nature without taking our sin, and the resurrection would destroy the man to remove the sin. The 1689 Confession confesses that corruption of nature remains in the regenerate, but the person and the corruption are not the same. The recovery holds both: no surrender in a time of confession, and no confusion of the sinner with his sin.
roots_summary: Greek hupotage (G5292), subjection; eiko (G1502), to give place, yield; oikeo (G3611), to dwell.
roots_lines: Greek eiko (G1502) — to yield, give place; Galatians 2:5, the only use.
usage: “no, not for an hour” (Gal 2:5) — Flacius against the Interims.
“Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1) — why a ceremony can become a surrender.
“sin that dwelleth in me” (Rom 7:17) — the distinction Flacius lost.

pos: n. (Nicholas von Amsdorf, 1483–1565, Luther's colleague and friend, first Protestant bishop of Naumburg, who in controversy said that good works are harmful to salvation)
etymology: German noble surname, from Amsdorf near Wurzen in Saxony.
biblical_def: Nicholas von Amsdorf was one of Luther's earliest colleagues at Wittenberg and among his most loyal friends. He rode with Luther to Worms in 1521 and was in the carriage when the elector's horsemen carried Luther off to the Wartburg. Luther consecrated him bishop of Naumburg in 1542, the first evangelical bishop in Germany, though he was driven out within a few years. After Luther's death he became a leader of the strict party. When Georg Major taught that good works are necessary to salvation, Amsdorf answered in 1559 that good works are harmful to salvation. He meant to defend justification by faith alone, and Paul's “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9). But Paul in the next breath says believers are “created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them” (Eph 2:10), and tells Titus to affirm constantly that “they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works” (Tit 3:8). The Formula of Concord rejected both Major's and Amsdorf's formulas: works are not necessary to salvation as its cause, and are not harmful to it, but are the necessary fruit of faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines works, in theology, as moral duties or external performances, as distinct from grace or faith.
webster_full: WORK, n. Effort; labour; employment.
2. In theology, works are moral duties or external performances, as distinct from grace or faith.
scriptures: Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Eph 2:10
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
Tit 3:8

This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.
Jas 2:18
Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.
corruption_summary: Amsdorf's slogan that good works harm salvation is the antinomian overcorrection, and its modern form is the grace that never asks for obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: Every defence of justification by faith faces the temptation Amsdorf yielded to: to protect grace by speaking of works as a threat. The modern versions are gentler — preaching that never calls believers to obey for fear of legalism, a horror of the word duty, a gospel of acceptance with no call to holiness. They share Amsdorf's instinct and his error.

The 1689 Confession puts works in their place: good works done in obedience to God's commandments are the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith, by which believers manifest their thankfulness and glorify God. They are not the root of salvation; they are its fruit, and a tree without fruit is not alive. The recovery is Paul's order in Ephesians 2: not of works, but unto good works.
roots_summary: Greek ergon (G2041), work; poiema (G4161), workmanship; phrontizo (G5431), to be careful.
roots_lines: Greek poiema (G4161) — that which is made, workmanship; Ephesians 2:10.
Greek phrontizo (G5431) — to give careful thought; Titus 3:8, the only use.
usage: “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9) — what Amsdorf rightly defended.
“created in Christ Jesus unto good works” (Eph 2:10) — what he forgot.
“careful to maintain good works” (Tit 3:8) — Paul's answer to the slogan.

pos: n. (Wolfgang Musculus, 1497–1563, Benedictine monk turned Reformed pastor at Augsburg and professor at Bern, whose Common Places were among the first Reformed systems to give the covenant a structural place)
biblical_def: Wolfgang Musculus was a Benedictine monk in Lorraine who read Luther, left the cloister, married, and worked as a weaver and ditch-digger at Strasbourg while studying under Bucer. He became pastor in Augsburg in 1531 and laboured there seventeen years, until the emperor's Interim drove him out. From 1549 he was professor of theology at Bern. His Common Places of Sacred Theology (1560), soon translated into English, were widely read by the Elizabethan clergy. Musculus gave unusual attention to the covenant, treating God's dealings with man as a covenant from Abraham to Christ, on the word of Genesis: “I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee” (Gen 17:7), fulfilled in the new covenant, “I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts” (Heb 8:10). He wrote commentaries on much of Scripture and held to Paul's charge, “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13). The psalm sums up the comfort he found in the doctrine: “The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant” (Psa 25:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines common-place as a memorandum; and, as a noun, a common topic; and a common-place book as a book in which are registered such facts, opinions or observations as are deemed worthy of notice.
webster_full: COMMON-PLACE, n. A memorandum; a common topic.
COMMON-PLACE BOOK, n. A book in which are registered such facts, opinions or observations as are deemed worthy of notice or remembrance, so disposed that any one may be easily found.
scriptures: Gen 17:7
And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee.
Heb 8:10

For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, saith the Lord; I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts: and I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people:
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant.
corruption_summary: Musculus belongs to the early shaping of covenant theology, and the modern habit of treating federal theology as a seventeenth-century invention erases men like him.
corruption_paragraphs: Critics of Reformed theology sometimes say covenant theology was a rigid scholastic system imposed on Scripture by later generations, distorting the warm biblical theology of the Reformers. Musculus, writing in the 1550s from long pastoral labour, already organised his theology around God's covenant with Abraham and its fulfilment in Christ. The covenant was not an invention of the schools; it was the shape of the Bible's own story.

The 1689 Confession's chapter on God's covenant stands in that line, confessing that it pleased the Lord to make a covenant of grace, revealed first in the promise and fully in the New Testament. Baptist readers part with Musculus on the sign of the covenant, as the Particular Baptists did, but receive his insight that God is pleased to bind Himself to His people by promise.
roots_summary: Hebrew berith (H1285), covenant; sod (H5475), secret, intimate counsel; Greek hupotuposis (G5296), form, pattern.
usage: “for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee” (Gen 17:7) — the thread of Musculus's theology.
“I will put my laws into their mind” (Heb 8:10) — the covenant fulfilled.
“he will shew them his covenant” (Psa 25:14) — the comfort of the doctrine.

pos: n. (Andreas Gerhard Hyperius, 1511–1564, Flemish-born professor at Marburg, whose treatise on the forming of sermons founded Protestant homiletics as a discipline)
etymology: Latin Hyperius, from Ypres in Flanders, his birthplace.
biblical_def: Andreas Hyperius studied at Paris and Louvain, travelled in Germany and England, and from 1541 taught theology at Marburg for the rest of his life. He is remembered chiefly for On the Forming of Sacred Sermons (1553), the first full Protestant treatise on preaching, which taught ministers to fit their exposition to the needs of their hearers: doctrine, reproof, instruction, correction and consolation, following Paul's own list. Its premise was Paul's charge: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2). Its model was Ezra's Levites, who “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense” (Neh 8:8), and its aim Paul's: “warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Col 1:28). He also wrote on the right ordering of theological study, sketching what later ages called a theological encyclopedia. The preacher's standard he set was Peter's: “If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God” (1Pe 4:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sermon as a discourse delivered in public by a licensed clergyman, for the purpose of religious instruction, and grounded on some text or passage of Scripture.
webster_full: SERMON, n. A discourse delivered in public by a licensed clergyman, for the purpose of religious instruction, and usually grounded on some text or passage of Scripture.
2. A printed discourse.
scriptures: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:

If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God; if any man minister, let him do it as of the ability which God giveth: that God in all things may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
corruption_summary: Hyperius made preaching a discipline to be learned under the authority of Scripture; modern homiletics often keeps the technique and loses the authority.
corruption_paragraphs: Hyperius taught method because he believed the preacher carried God's Word to God's people and must not mishandle it. Much modern homiletics has inherited his attention to the hearer while abandoning his premise, so that sermons are built around felt needs and the text is consulted for illustrations. The application has swallowed the doctrine.

The recovery is Hyperius's order: the text first, its sense given distinctly, and then the sense applied to the hearers for doctrine, reproof, correction and comfort. A sermon should speak as the oracles of God; method serves that, and nothing else.
roots_summary: Greek kerusso (G2784), to preach; noutheteo (G3560), to warn, admonish; logion (G3051), oracle.
roots_lines: Greek noutheteo (G3560) — to put in mind, warn; Colossians 1:28.
Greek logion (G3051) — an utterance of God, oracle; 1 Peter 4:11, Romans 3:2.
usage: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — the charge behind Hyperius's book.
“gave the sense” (Neh 8:8) — the first duty of the sermon.
“let him speak as the oracles of God” (1Pe 4:11) — the preacher's standard.

pos: n. (François Lambert of Avignon, 1487–1530, former Franciscan who drafted the congregational church order of the Homberg Synod in 1526 and was the first professor of theology at Marburg, where he taught Patrick Hamilton)
biblical_def: Lambert of Avignon was a Franciscan preacher who came to the Reformation through reading Luther, left his order in 1522, and went to Zwingli at Zurich and then to Wittenberg, where he married. Philip of Hesse called him to help reform his territory, and at the Synod of Homberg in October 1526 Lambert presented a church order of remarkable boldness. Each congregation was to be a gathering of professing believers who had given their names; they were to elect their own bishops, that is pastors, and deacons; they were to exercise discipline and excommunication themselves, after Christ's rule, “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17); and a yearly synod of pastors and delegates was to oversee the whole. He appealed to the apostolic pattern: “when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23); the brethren were to “look ye out among you seven men of honest report” (Act 6:3). On Luther's advice the landgrave never put the order into force. Lambert became the first professor of theology at the new University of Marburg in 1527, and the young Scot Patrick Hamilton studied under him before going home to die. Lambert died of plague in 1530.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines synod as an ecclesiastical council or meeting to consult on church matters.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. In church history, a council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
2. A meeting, convention or council.
scriptures: And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Act 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: Lambert's Homberg order was an early Protestant attempt at a believers' church governed by its own elected officers, and it was shelved for the same reasons that keep such churches suspect today.
corruption_paragraphs: Luther advised against the Homberg order because he thought the people unready, and because the territorial church was the only form of order he trusted. The same judgment has persisted: a church of professing believers who choose their own officers and exercise discipline is thought impractical, divisive or sectarian. Lambert, a former friar who had seen the old system's corruption, thought it was simply the New Testament.

The 1689 Confession confesses that each church, gathered according to Christ's mind, has power to choose its own elders and deacons, and that the members are saints by calling who have given themselves to the Lord and to one another. The Particular Baptists found in that pattern what Lambert proposed at Homberg. The recovery is the gathered, disciplined, self-governing congregation under Christ.
roots_summary: Greek cheirotoneo (G5500), to ordain by vote, appoint; episkopeo (G1983), to take the oversight; sunago (G4863), to gather together.
roots_lines: Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to choose by stretching out the hand, ordain; Acts 14:23, 2 Corinthians 8:19.
Greek episkopeo (G1983) — to oversee, take the oversight; 1 Peter 5:2.
usage: “when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — the Homberg pattern.
“look ye out among you seven men of honest report” (Act 6:3) — the congregation choosing its officers.
“where two or three are gathered together in my name” (Mat 18:20) — the church gathered under Christ.

pos: n. (Caspar Schwenckfeld von Ossig, 1489–1561, Silesian nobleman and spiritualist reformer who suspended the Lord's Supper and taught that Christ's human flesh was uncreated)
etymology: German noble surname. His followers, the Schwenkfelders, settled in Pennsylvania in 1734.
biblical_def: Caspar Schwenckfeld was a Silesian courtier converted through Luther's writings who became a lay preacher of great earnestness. Troubled by the bitter quarrels over the Supper and by the lack of change in the lives of communicants, he and his circle announced in 1526 a Stillstand, a suspension of the Lord's Supper until God should give clarity, and they never resumed it. He taught that true faith comes by the inner Word, of which the outward Scripture is only the witness, and that the flesh of Christ was not a creature but was progressively deified, so that the believer feeds inwardly on a heavenly flesh. Luther, Zwingli and Calvin all rejected him. Hebrews answers his Christology: “Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same” (Heb 2:14), for “in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren” (Heb 2:17); the Mediator is “the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). And Christ's institution answers the Stillstand: “this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19). He lived as a wanderer, protected by friendly nobles, and died at Ulm.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spiritualism as the state of being spiritual; and, in philosophy, the doctrine that all which exists is spirit or soul.
webster_full: SPIRITUALISM, n. The state of being spiritual.
2. In philosophy, the doctrine in opposition to the materialists, that all which exists is spirit or soul.
scriptures: Heb 2:14

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;
Heb 2:17

Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
corruption_summary: Schwenckfeld's suspension of the Supper and his inner-word piety anticipate every modern Christianity that trusts private spirituality above the ordinances Christ appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: Schwenckfeld's motives were sympathetic: grief over division and over unchanged lives. His remedy was to withdraw from the outward means into an inward communion, and modern Christianity is full of his heirs — believers who think the Lord's Table optional, who find God more readily in private experience than in the preached Word, who regard church as one resource among many for the spiritual life. Spiritualism always presents itself as a deeper devotion.

The recovery is the Reformed doctrine of the means of grace. Christ instituted His Word, baptism and the Supper as the ordinary means by which the Spirit works, and the 1689 Confession calls the Supper an ordinance to be observed in His churches unto the end of the world. Nor is His flesh a heavenly substance; He took our nature, made like His brethren in all things, sin excepted, so that He could be a merciful and faithful high priest.
roots_summary: Greek metecho (G3348), to take part, partake; homoioo (G3666), to make like; mesites (G3316), mediator.
roots_lines: Greek metecho (G3348) — to share, take part of; Hebrews 2:14.
usage: “he also himself likewise took part of the same” (Heb 2:14) — against an uncreated flesh.
“the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5) — the Mediator is truly man.
“this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19) — against the Stillstand of 1526.

pos: n. (Hans Denck, c. 1500–1527, humanist schoolmaster expelled from Nuremberg, Anabaptist and spiritualist teacher, co-translator of the Hebrew Prophets into German, suspected of universalism)
etymology: German personal name. With Ludwig Hätzer he produced the Worms Prophets of 1527.
biblical_def: Hans Denck was a gifted young humanist, rector of the school of St Sebald in Nuremberg, who was examined by the city's Lutheran preachers in 1525 and expelled for unsound views. He joined the Anabaptists, was baptized by Hubmaier at Augsburg, and travelled through south Germany teaching and baptizing. With Ludwig Hätzer he translated the Hebrew Prophets into German (Worms, 1527), a careful work that preceded Luther's own. Christ had shown that the Prophets speak of Him: “beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27). But Denck increasingly taught that the inner Word in every man is the true teacher and the outward Scripture only its witness, and he was widely charged with holding that all men, and even the devil, would at last be saved. Scripture closes both doors: “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19), and “these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal” (Mat 25:46). Sick and weary, he wrote a statement at Basel in 1527 qualifying some of his views, and died of plague there at about twenty-seven.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines universalist as one who holds the doctrine of the salvation of all men.
webster_full: UNIVERSALIST, n. One who holds the doctrine that all men will be saved.
UNIVERSALISM, n. The doctrine of the final salvation of all men.
scriptures: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Denck is admired by modern liberal theology as a tolerant mystic ahead of his time, and the admiration is for exactly what was wrong: an inner word above Scripture and a hope of universal salvation.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal historians found in Denck a precursor of their own convictions: a gentle spiritualist who refused to persecute, trusted the divine spark in every soul, and hoped all would be saved. His personal gentleness is real and his translation of the Prophets is a genuine achievement. But the inner word that judges Scripture and the hope that hell will at last be emptied are the two pillars of modern liberal Christianity, and both deny what Christ taught.

The recovery is the sufficiency and clarity of Scripture, the more sure word of prophecy to which we do well to take heed, and the honest acceptance of Christ's own words about everlasting punishment. The 1689 Confession confesses that the wicked shall be cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord.
roots_summary: Greek diermeneuo (G1329), to expound, interpret; bebaioteros (cf. bebaios, G949), more sure; aionios (G166), everlasting.
roots_lines: Greek diermeneuo (G1329) — to explain thoroughly, expound; Luke 24:27.
usage: “he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) — the Prophets Denck translated.
“a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19) — against the inner word.
“everlasting punishment” (Mat 25:46) — against the hope of an empty hell.

pos: n. (Felix Manz, c. 1498–1527, Zurich Hebrew scholar in whose mother's house the first believer's baptisms of the Reformation were performed, drowned in the Limmat by the Zurich council)
etymology: Swiss German surname. Remembered as the first martyr of the Swiss Brethren at the hands of Protestant authorities.
biblical_def: Felix Manz was the son of a Zurich canon, a learned Hebraist who studied the Scriptures with Zwingli and Conrad Grebel. In the house of his mother on 21 January 1525 the first baptisms on confession of faith took place. He preached and baptized in the countryside, was arrested again and again, and refused to promise silence. In March 1526 the Zurich council made rebaptism punishable by drowning, and on 5 January 1527 Manz was taken in a boat onto the Limmat, his hands bound over his knees, and thrown into the river. His mother and brother stood on the bank urging him to remain faithful. As he was pushed under he cried out the words of Christ on the cross, “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luk 23:46). The magistrates mocked believer's baptism as a third baptism by water. Manz had been baptized into Christ's death according to Paul, “buried with him by baptism into death” (Rom 6:4), and he kept the word of Revelation, “be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10). “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psa 116:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to drown as to overwhelm in water; to suffocate or extinguish life by immersion in water or other fluid.
webster_full: DROWN, v.t. To overwhelm in water; to submerge; to inundate.
2. To suffocate or extinguish life by immersion in water or other fluid.
scriptures: And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost.
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
corruption_summary: Manz was drowned by a Reformed city council for believer's baptism, and Reformed Baptists must remember both that he was right about baptism and that his judges were wrong about the sword.
corruption_paragraphs: Reformed histories long passed over Manz in silence or mentioned him only as a disturber of the peace. Anabaptist histories rightly honour him and sometimes conclude that the whole Reformed tradition is discredited by Zurich's council. The 1689 Baptists inherit both parts of that history: the confession of Zwingli's Zurich on grace and Scripture, and the conviction of Manz's circle on baptism and the gathered church.

The recovery is honesty. The Zurich council sinned in drowning a believer for his baptism; the 1689 Confession's teaching on liberty of conscience condemns what it did. And Manz was right to baptize believers only, as the Confession also confesses. He died praying the words of the Saviour, and the Lord counted his death precious.
roots_summary: Greek paratithemi (G3908), to commit, entrust; sunthapto (G4916), to bury with; Hebrew yaqar (H3368), precious.
roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to deposit, commit to one's charge; Luke 23:46.
usage: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luk 23:46) — Manz's cry on the Limmat.
“buried with him by baptism into death” (Rom 6:4) — the baptism he died for.
“Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psa 116:15) — 5 January 1527.

pos: n. (Fulgentius of Ruspe, c. 465–c. 530, North African bishop exiled to Sardinia by the Arian Vandal king Thrasamund, the most faithful defender of Augustine's doctrine of grace in the generation after him)
etymology: Latin Fulgentius, from fulgeo, to shine. Ruspe was a coastal town in Byzacena, modern Tunisia.
biblical_def: Fulgentius was a tax official of noble family who became a monk and, around 507, bishop of Ruspe, under the Vandal kings who ruled Africa and favoured Arianism. Thrasamund banished him with some sixty other Catholic bishops to Sardinia, where they lived in community, studied and wrote; the king later recalled him for debate and banished him again. He returned only when Hilderic allowed the exiles home in 523. His writings defended the Trinity against the Arians and Augustine's doctrine of grace against Faustus of Riez and the Semi-Pelagians of Gaul. He taught that God's election is gratuitous, not founded on foreseen merit: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy” (Rom 9:15); God has predestinated His people “according to the good pleasure of his will” (Eph 1:5), and there is “a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5). He held that God predestines the wicked to the punishment their sins deserve, never to the sin itself. In exile he could say with Paul, “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). His books were read by Gottschalk, by the Reformers, and by the Reformed orthodox as a witness that Augustine's doctrine did not die with him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exile as the state of being expelled from one's native country or place of residence by authority, and forbidden to return.
webster_full: EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country or place of residence by authority, and forbid to return, either for a limited time or for perpetuity.
2. An abandonment of one's country, or removal to a foreign country for residence.
scriptures: Rom 9:15
For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.
Eph 1:5
Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will,
Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
corruption_summary: Fulgentius shows that Augustine's doctrine of grace had faithful heirs before the Reformation; the claim that the early church knew nothing of sovereign election ignores the African bishops in Sardinia.
corruption_paragraphs: A common objection to Reformed soteriology is that it is Augustine's innovation, abandoned by the church after him and revived only by Calvin. Fulgentius answers it. A generation after Augustine, under persecution by Arian kings, he and his fellow exiles taught gratuitous election, the priority of grace and the distinction between God's decree to save and His just reprobation of sinners for their sins. The Council of Orange in 529 owed much to that African line.

The recovery is a fuller church history. The doctrine of the 1689 Confession on God's decree is not a sixteenth-century peculiarity but the faith of bishops who wrote it in exile with their lives at stake. The word of God was not bound in Sardinia, and it is not bound now.
roots_summary: Greek eleeo (G1653), to have mercy; eudokia (G2107), good pleasure; leimma (G3005), remnant.
roots_lines: Greek leimma (G3005) — a remnant; Romans 11:5, the only use.
usage: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy” (Rom 9:15) — gratuitous election in the African church.
“a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) — the doctrine of the exiles.
“the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9) — Sardinia, c. 510.
